html:
The First Battle of the Marne was fought from 5 to 12 September 1914 along the Marne River east of Paris, in France. French and British armies stopped the German advance and forced it to retreat.

Germany planned to win World War I fast: beat France in six weeks by marching through Belgium, then turn on Russia. By early September its armies were about 50 km from Paris. But the German right wing turned to pass east of the city, showing its side to the French there. The French commander Joseph Joffre ordered a counter-attack. A new army struck from Paris, some of its men sent out in taxis. A gap opened between two German armies, and the British moved into it. The Germans pulled back about 60 km to the Aisne River and dug in. About two million men fought, and each side lost roughly a quarter of a million.

The plan for a short war had failed. Each side tried to get around the other to the north, and by the end of 1914 trenches ran from Switzerland to the sea. France was saved, and Germany faced a long war on two fronts; see Tannenberg and Verdun.
